title: TASS vs. Infectious Endophthalmitis: A Diagnostic Divide
summary: Toxic Anterior Segment Syndrome (TASS) and postoperative endophthalmitis represent the two most feared acute inflammatory complications following intraocular surgery. Mastering their rapid differentiation is critical for sight-saving management.

sections.title: TASS vs. Endophthalmitis: Key Clinical Differentiators
TASS Red Flags
content: Inability to visualize the posterior pole (requires tap)
Decreasing visual acuity after initial stabilization

rows: Strands through wound; risk of endophthalmitis

content.explanation: P: Preservatives (e.g., BAC), I: Impurities (endotoxins), P: pH/Osmolality mismatch, E: Enzymatic residues, S: Sterilizing agents.

sections.title: Management Algorithm
content: Step 1: Clinical index of suspicion (Early vs Late onset).
Step 2: If vitritis exists: Emergent Vitreous Tap/Biopsy.
Step 4: If TASS suspected: Aggressive topical Steroids (Prednisolone Acetate 1% q1h).
Step 5: Monitor IOP and repeat culture/Tap if no improvement at 24-48h.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: TASS is an inflammatory response to non-infectious substances; it is non-infectious by definition.
Any vitreous haze essentially rules out TASS and confirms Endophthalmitis until proven otherwise.
Always inspect the surgical logs/sterilization logs when a TASS cluster occurs.
The EVS (Endophthalmitis Vitrectomy Study) remains the gold standard for treatment guidelines regarding vitrectomy vs. tap/inject.
Post-operative pain is the patient's most reliable symptom for early infection.
